name: Yvoire Classic / Contour / Volume

card.summary: A range of Korean hyaluronic acid fillers from LG Chem, used by clinicians to smooth lines and add volume to the cheeks, chin, nose and lips.
card.note: Injectable; performed by licensed clinicians. Filler complications can include vascular events.

quick.overview:
Yvoire is a brand of hyaluronic acid (HA) dermal fillers made by LG Chem. The Classic, Contour and Volume versions are designed for different depths: finer lines in the mid-dermis, and deeper volume or contouring work.

In trials, Yvoire Classic and Volume were compared with Restylane and Perlane for nasolabial folds, and a midface product, Y-Solution 720, produced improvement in midface volume in most treated participants at 26 weeks.
quick.how: A clinician injects the gel at the depth and site suited to the goal, such as the nasolabial folds, midface, chin or nose. Clinical papers describe planning by facial proportion, line and angle, especially in East Asian patients. HA fillers are temporary and can be dissolved with hyaluronidase.
quick.risks: Common filler effects include swelling, bruising and redness. Rare vascular complications such as tissue necrosis can occur, which is why clinicians keep hyaluronidase available. Treatments are medical procedures delivered by licensed practitioners.

lead: Yvoire is a line of hyaluronic acid (HA) dermal fillers developed by the Korean company LG Chem. Variants such as Classic, Volume and Contour are matched to different injection depths and uses, from mid-dermal lines to deeper volumising and contouring, and a newer product, Y-Solution 720, is designed for the midface.[1][2][7]

For appearance, the fillers are used by clinicians to soften nasolabial folds and marionette lines, restore cheek volume, and add projection or definition to features such as the nose, chin and forehead, so that the face reads as fuller, smoother or better proportioned. Several clinical papers describe planning Yvoire treatments around East Asian facial proportions and the features many patients in the region ask about, such as a low nasal bridge, a flat midface and a small chin.[3][4]

Published studies include randomized split-face trials against Restylane and Perlane, a randomized midface trial of Y-Solution 720, and a two-year 3D volume study that included Yvoire Contour.[2][6][7] Like other HA fillers, the products are temporary and can be broken down with the enzyme hyaluronidase.[5][8]

angle.text: A clinician places the gel where volume or support is wanted. Results are temporary and typically last months.

paras: Yvoire is the brand name LG Chem uses for its hyaluronic acid fillers. HA is a sugar-based molecule naturally present in skin; in fillers it is chemically cross-linked into a gel that holds water and stays in the tissue for months. A general reference on injectable fillers notes that HA products are among the most common because the body already contains HA, that most are cross-linked with a compound called BDDE to last longer, and that most wrinkle fillers of this kind are temporary, often lasting about six months.[8][9]

The Yvoire range is described in trials by its rheology, meaning how firm and cohesive the gel is. The authors of two nasolabial-fold trials state that Yvoire Classic has rheological properties similar to Restylane and suits mid-dermis injection, while Yvoire Volume resembles Perlane and suits deep-dermis injection for deeper folds.[7] Yvoire Contour and Yvoire Volume Plus appear in studies of cheek volumising and lip augmentation, and Y-Solution 720 was developed for midface volume loss.[2][5][6]

A distinction used in the filler literature is between monophasic gels, which are smooth and uniform, and biphasic gels, which are made of gel particles in a carrier. The two-year cheek study classified Yvoire Contour as biphasic and compared it with monophasic products.[6]

Yvoire Classic and Volume were tested in the nasolabial folds, the creases running from the nose to the corners of the mouth, where filler is meant to make the folds look shallower.[7] A pilot study of five East Asian women also described treating nasolabial folds and marionette lines with the aim of a natural-looking result.[3]

Midface volume loss, a flatter or more hollow cheek area, is the target of Y-Solution 720, which was tested in Asian participants with mild to severe volume deficit.[2] Contour products are used to add projection in the anteromedial cheek, the area just beside the nose and under the eye, and a split-face study measured how much of that added volume remained over two years.[6]

Authors of an expert consensus paper, a group of five plastic surgeons convened as the YVOIRE Consensus Group, wrote that Chinese faces are often characterised by a retruded forehead and chin and a low nasal bridge, that profile features strongly influence perceived attractiveness, and that younger patients especially ask for nose and chin augmentation.[4] They described injection approaches meant to produce results consistent with these characteristics, such as a long, slender face and a pointed chin.[4] The 2025 pilot study proposed three named approaches, Balance-L for outer contour lines, Balance-A for profile angles and Balance-P for facial proportions, and showed five treated patients as examples.[3]
Yvoire Volume Plus is among the lip fillers compared in a laboratory study of how quickly hyaluronidase breaks down different products.[5]

The fillers are supplied as pre-filled syringes and are injected by clinicians, with the product and depth chosen to suit the area: finer, more flexible gels for lines and firmer gels for deeper volume or projection.[7][3] Regulators describe dermal fillers as medical devices that should be injected by licensed providers trained in dermatology or plastic surgery, and the US FDA advises people not to self-inject or buy fillers online.[9]

Treatments are temporary. In the nasolabial fold trials the correcting effect was reported for up to 26 weeks, and in the midface trial most participants still showed improvement at 52 weeks after the last injection.[2][7] Patients who want to keep the result return for repeat treatments, a point common to HA fillers generally.[8]

Nasolabial folds: Two similarly designed split-face, evaluator-blind, noninferiority studies enrolled 58 subjects (Yvoire Classic versus Restylane) and 57 subjects (Yvoire Volume versus Perlane) with moderate-to-severe folds. At week 26 the mean Wrinkle Severity Rating Scale scores were 2.56 for both Classic and Restylane, and 2.89 versus 2.91 for Volume and Perlane; the authors concluded the Yvoire products were noninferior, with similar safety and satisfaction.[7]

Midface volume: In a multicenter, randomized, evaluator-blind trial, Asian participants with midface volume loss received Y-Solution 720 (173 participants) or no treatment (65 participants). At week 26, 82.0% of treated participants improved by at least one grade on the Midface Volume Deficit Severity Rating Scale for Asian Faces, versus 5.1% of controls, and 76.2% were still improved at week 52. Swelling, tenderness and pain were the common treatment-site responses and were mild and transient.[2]

Two-year cheek volume: A split-face study of adults aged 30 to 50 used 3D scanning to follow cheek volume after injection of Belotero Volume on one side and a control filler, including Yvoire Contour, on the other. The two monophasic fillers kept 81 percent and 66 percent of their volume at two years relative to week 4, while the two biphasic fillers, Yvoire Contour and Restylane SubQ, kept more than 50 percent; the authors reported that both types showed efficacy, safety and durability.[6]

Technique papers: The Balance-technique pilot reported on five East Asian women and called for further study.[3] The consensus paper is based on the experience of five surgeons and the peer-reviewed literature rather than a trial.[4]

Other: A phase III randomized trial of 72 patients compared the polynucleotide product Rejuran with Yvoire-Hydro for crow's feet using a split-face design; Yvoire served as the comparator, and the publication is listed as retracted.[1]

Common reactions to HA fillers include bruising, redness, swelling, pain and itching; less common are nodules, infection and allergic reactions.[8][9] The most concerning risk described by the FDA is unintentional injection into a blood vessel, which can block blood supply and cause tissue death, vision problems including blindness, stroke and, rarely, death.[9] The FDA tells providers to stop injecting if signs such as blanching, vision change or unusual pain appear and to have a plan for vascular complications.[9]

Because HA can be degraded by hyaluronidase, clinicians use the enzyme to dissolve filler in an emergency or when a result is unwanted. A 2026 laboratory study incubated six lip fillers, including Yvoire Volume Plus, with hyaluronidase and found significant differences in breakdown rate between products, with Restylane Kysse breaking down fastest, followed by Yvoire Volume Plus and Neauvia Intense Lips.[5]

In the United States, the FDA regulates fillers as medical devices and approves specific products for specific areas; in the UK and European Economic Area they are CE-marked devices.[8][9] The FDA has said that fillers in some areas, such as the nose, forehead and around the eyes, are not approved uses.[9] The clinical literature cited here for Yvoire comes largely from East Asian studies.

South Korea has a large cosmetic-procedure industry. Wikipedia reports a 2021 market value of about US$1.95 billion and rising numbers of medical tourists, and it describes facial contouring as a common goal of procedures in the country.[11]

Other HA fillers compared against Yvoire in trials include Restylane, Perlane, Juvederm and Belotero.[6][7] Polynucleotide skin boosters such as Rejuran are a separate category aimed at skin quality.[1] Surgical alternatives for contour changes include implants and fat grafting, and facial-contouring surgeries such as jaw and cheekbone reduction are also common in Korea.[11]

timeline.event: Karl Meyer and John Palmer first isolate hyaluronic acid from the vitreous of a cow's eye, the starting point for later HA medical products.[10]
A phase III trial of Rejuran versus Yvoire-Hydro for crow's feet is published in the Journal of Korean Medical Science (later listed as retracted).[1]
Two randomized trials of Yvoire Classic and Volume in nasolabial folds, and an expert consensus paper from the YVOIRE Consensus Group on Chinese patients, are published.[7][4]
Two-year 3D split-face cheek volume study that included Yvoire Contour is published.[6]
Pilot study of Balance injection techniques with Yvoire in East Asian patients is published.[3]
Randomized midface trial of Y-Solution 720 and a laboratory study of hyaluronidase breakdown of lip fillers including Yvoire Volume Plus are published.[2][5]
